readerTitle: You have $10M of profit. Where should it go?
caseNote: 가상 시뮬레이션 (지역 냉난방·배관 서비스 회사 + 부품 유통업체 인수 제안) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 이익을 어디에 쓸지는 '좋은 사업인가'가 아니라 '투자한 1달러가 기준 수익률을 넘는가'로 정하고, 기준을 넘는 곳이 없으면 주주에게 돌려주는 것도 좋은 배분이다.
misconception: 이익이 나는 좋은 사업이면 사들이는 게 맞고, 남은 현금은 어떻게든 회사 안에서 써야 한다.

sources.text: 기업재무의 표준 개념 (투하자본수익률, 기준 수익률, 재투자·환원 결정)

factChecks.note: 유통업체: $8M에 연 $600K → 7.5%. $5M이면 600 ÷ 5,000 = 12%로 기준과 같음. $8M 인수 시 $5.5M만 남아 있으므로 $2.5M 부족(차입 필요).
본사 건물: $6M, 연 임대료 절감 $240K → 4%. $5.5M 대비 $0.5M 부족. 3단계 배분: 예비자금 $1.5M + 주주 배당 $4M = $5.5M.
12% 기준 수익률은 설명용 가정입니다. '비슷한 위험에서 주주가 다른 곳에서 기대할 수 있는 수준'이라는 설명은 일반 원리로만 썼습니다. 신규 지점이 자리 잡는 데 2~3년이 걸린다는 문장은 일반적 표현이며 특정 통계가 아닙니다.

cards.title: Five people, one $10M decision
body: You run a home services company: heating, cooling and plumbing across a region. This year it earned $10M after tax, and the cash is sitting in the bank.
By Monday, people across the company have asked for it. Their requests add up to almost twice what you have.

image.label: A desk with a stack of cash and many outstretched hands
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 책상 위에 '$10M'이라고 적힌 돈 더미 하나, 그 주변으로 작업복·정장·안전조끼를 입은 손 다섯 개가 서류를 내밀고 있음. 실제 기업 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: The asks on your desk
body: You've set one rule: a project should earn at least **12% a year** on the money it uses. That's roughly what the owners could expect elsewhere for similar risk.
list: **Buy a parts distributor** with a warehouse and trucks: $8M
**A new head office** with a showroom: $6M
**Pay the owners** a dividend: any amount
cards.callout: Total asks: $18.5M plus the dividend. You have $10M.
cards.softwareNote: A software company faces the same desk: hire another product team, buy a smaller rival, or return cash to shareholders. The same tests apply.

cards.title: How do you rank the asks?
body: Each branch costs $1.5M and, based on your current branches, earns about $375K a year once established. The distributor would add $600K a year. The office would save $240K a year in rent.

options.text: Rank by how much yearly profit each one adds
options.feedback: The distributor wins at $600K, but it needs $8M to get there. Ranking by dollars alone favors big projects, not good ones.

options.text: Rank by yearly profit per dollar invested
options.feedback: Branches earn 25%, the distributor 7.5%, the office 4%. Now you can see which money works hardest.

options.text: Start with the office. The team is cramped and morale matters
options.feedback: The pain is real, but it isn't the test. You'd lock $6M into a 4% return before checking anything better.

cards.title: The distributor's owner calls.
body: Say you chose to rank by return per dollar. Branches clear your 12% bar easily, so you fund all three: $4.5M. That leaves $5.5M.
Now the distributor's owner presses. It's a solid, profitable business, and owning it would secure your parts supply. The price: $8M for $600K a year.

options.text: Buy it. It's profitable, and supply matters
options.feedback: You'd borrow $2.5M to close and tie $8M to a 7.5% return, below your bar. A good business at the wrong price is a poor use of capital.

options.text: Decline politely and keep buying parts from them
options.feedback: You keep the supply without owning the warehouse, and $5.5M stays free for something that clears your bar.
At $5M, $600K is exactly 12%, so the math works. But the seller may refuse, and a deal that barely clears the bar leaves no room for mistakes.

cards.title: What about the last $5.5M?
body: Say you passed on the distributor. You've checked: only these three towns have enough demand and staff for a strong branch. Any further branch looks closer to 8%.

options.text: Build the head office. The cash is right there
options.feedback: That's $6M at 4%, and you'd still be $500K short. The owners could earn far more on that money elsewhere.

options.text: Keep $1.5M for a slow season and pay $4M to the owners
options.feedback: The reserve protects the business. The owners can put $4M to work at returns you can't offer them right now.

options.text: Keep all $5.5M in the bank until a better idea comes
options.feedback: Safe, and sometimes wise. But bank interest sits well below 12%, and idle cash tends to attract weaker projects later.

cards.title: Where the $10M went

breakdown.label: Three branches
breakdown.detail: About 25% return, roughly $1.125M a year once established

cards.callout: Two of the four asks got nothing. Every dollar went to its best use, including back to the owners.
cards.softwareNote: In a software company, the same breakdown might fund one team with clear returns, keep runway in reserve, and skip an acquisition priced below the bar.

cards.title: The numbers are estimates, not facts.
body: New branches can take two or three years to reach full profit, and some never do. Check results against the plan each year.
The 12% bar is a judgment. Set it too high and you starve good projects. Set it too low and you fund weak ones.
And **strategic value** can be real. If parts shortages were costing you jobs, put a number on it. Don't let the word alone carry the decision.

cards.title: Every dollar of profit needs a job worth doing.
body: Here's how your three choices map to this unit:
list: **Step 1, rank by return per dollar:** return on invested capital
**Step 2, decline the distributor:** hurdle rates, and saying no to good projects
**Step 3, pay out what you can't use well:** reinvest, return or acquire
cards.callout: **Try it today:** list your next three spending ideas. For each, write the money needed and the yearly profit it should bring. Divide. Which ones beat your bar?
